category: Functional Programming II: Operator Forms, Folds, Applies, Loops & Assignment Operators
description: Second tier of functional and procedural constructs: operator forms and currying (OperatorApplied, ReverseApplied, CurryApplied), Comap/ComapApply, MapApply and MapAll, the extended fold family (FoldPair, FoldWhile, SequenceFold), ArrayReduce, NestGraph, pattern-based AllMatch/AnyMatch/NoneMatch, first-match selectors, compound expressions and loop control (Break, Continue, Goto/Label), in-place assignment operators (AddTo, Increment, ApplyTo), Distribute, SlotSequence, Construct and Unique.

tools.name: MapApply
tools.description: MapApply[f, expr] (operator @@@) replaces the head of each element at level 1 by f - i.e. applies f to the arguments of each sublist - the idiom for calling a multi-argument function over a list of argument tuples. Clearer than Apply[f, expr, {1}] and available in operator form MapApply[f].
tools.usage:
MapApply[f, {{a1, b1}, {a2, b2}, ...}]
f @@@ list
MapApply[f][list]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function taking the elements of each sublist as separate arguments.

tools.name: MapAll
tools.description: MapAll[f, expr] (operator //@) applies f to every subexpression at every level, from the leaves upward, including the whole expression - a full traversal transform; Map with a level specification restricts levels, and Replace with rules is the pattern-based alternative.
tools.usage:
MapAll[f, expr]
f //@ expr
MapAll[f, expr, Heads -> True]
tools.example:
MapAll[g, a + b c] (* g[g[a] + g[g[b] g[c]]] *)
MapAll[If[NumberQ[#], N[#], #] &, expr] (* numericize every number *)

tools.name: OperatorApplied
tools.description: OperatorApplied[f][x][y] is f[y, x] (and OperatorApplied[f, n] / OperatorApplied[f, n -> m] generalize to n arguments with a chosen order) - a way to build operator forms of functions that lack them, matching the built-in convention where the data argument comes last; ReverseApplied[f] gives f with reversed argument order and CurryApplied[f, n] a fully curried form. Use them to build pipeline-friendly functions with // and Composition.
tools.usage:
OperatorApplied[f][x][y] (* f[y, x] *)
OperatorApplied[f, n][x1, ..., xn-1][y]
OperatorApplied[f, n -> {i1, i2, ...}]
ReverseApplied[f][x, y] (* f[y, x] *)
ReverseApplied[f, n]
CurryApplied[f, n][x1][x2]...[xn]
CurryApplied[f, {i1, i2, ...}]
tools.example:
subtractFrom10 = OperatorApplied[Subtract][10]; (* Subtract[y, 10] *)
{12, 15} // Map[subtractFrom10] (* {2, 5} *)
Sort[data, ReverseApplied[Less]] (* descending *)
CurryApplied[Plus, 3][1][2][3] (* 6 *)

tools.name: Comap
tools.description: Comap[{f1, f2, ...}, x] applies each function in a list to the same argument, giving {f1[x], f2[x], ...} (the dual of Map: many functions, one argument), and ComapApply applies each function to a sequence of arguments; they replace Through[{f1, f2}[x]] and Map[#[x] &, fs] with a clearer construct (14.0+). Ideal for computing several statistics of one dataset.
tools.usage:
Comap[{f1, f2, ...}, x]
Comap[{f1, f2, ...}][x]
ComapApply[{f1, f2, ...}, {x1, x2, ...}] (* fi[x1, x2, ...] *)
ComapApply[fs][args]
tools.example:
Comap[{Mean, Median, StandardDeviation}, data]
Comap[<|"min" -> Min, "max" -> Max|>, data] (* association of results *)
ComapApply[{Plus, Times, Max}, {2, 3}] (* {5, 6, 3} *)

tools.name: FoldPair
tools.description: FoldPair[f, y0, list] folds with a function returning {output, newState} pairs, collecting the outputs (and returning the final state with FoldPairList's cumulative form) - the standard pattern for stateful transformations such as running encoders, tokenizers and chunking by cumulative size without explicit loops; FoldPairList returns the list of outputs.
tools.usage:
FoldPair[f, y0, {x1, x2, ...}]
FoldPair[f, y0, list, g] (* g applied to final state *)
FoldPairList[f, y0, {x1, x2, ...}]
FoldPairList[f, y0, list, g]
tools.example:
(* running balance with per-step output *)
FoldPairList[{#1 + #2, #1 + #2} &, 0, {10, -3, 5}] (* {10, 7, 12} *)
(* cut a list into chunks whose totals do not exceed 10 *)
FoldPairList[Function[{acc, x}, If[acc + x > 10, {"cut", x}, {Nothing, acc + x}]], 0, {4, 5, 3, 6, 2}]

tools.name: FoldWhile
tools.description: FoldWhile[f, x, list, test] folds f over the list only while test remains True on the accumulated value, returning the last value that satisfied it; FoldWhileList returns all intermediate results. It is Fold with early termination - accumulating until a budget is exhausted, iterating until a tolerance is met - without Throw/Catch. Introduced in 13.1.
tools.usage:
FoldWhile[f, x, {a1, a2, ...}, test]
FoldWhile[f, {a1, a2, ...}, test]
FoldWhile[f, x, list, test, m] (* test on the last m results *)
FoldWhile[f, x, list, test, All]
FoldWhileList[f, x, list, test]

parameters.name: test
parameters.description: Predicate on the accumulated value (or last m values).

tools.example:
FoldWhile[Plus, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, # < 7 &] (* 6 *)
FoldWhileList[#1/2 &, 100, Range[20], # > 1 &] (* halve until below 1 *)

tools.name: SequenceFold
tools.description: SequenceFold[f, {y1, ..., yk}, {x1, x2, ...}] folds with a function of the last k results plus the next element - a fold with memory - and SequenceFoldList returns the whole sequence; it directly implements multi-term recurrences (Fibonacci-like), IIR filters and Markov-style updates from a seed sequence.
tools.usage:
SequenceFold[f, {y1, ..., yk}, {x1, x2, ...}]
SequenceFoldList[f, {y1, ..., yk}, {x1, x2, ...}]
tools.example:
SequenceFoldList[#1 + #2 &, {1, 1}, ConstantArray[Null, 8]] (* Fibonacci: {1,1,2,3,5,...} via f[y_{n-2}, y_{n-1}, x] *)
(* IIR filter y[n] = 0.5 y[n-1] + x[n] *)
SequenceFoldList[0.5 #1 + #2 &, {0}, signal]

tools.name: ArrayReduce
tools.description: Reduces an array along one or several dimensions by applying a function to the slices (e.g. Total or Max along axis 2, or a custom function of each column), the NumPy-style axis reduction that replaces Map/Transpose gymnastics; works with packed arrays, SparseArray and NumericArray. Introduced in 13.3.
tools.usage:
ArrayReduce[f, array, n]
ArrayReduce[f, array, {n1, n2}]
ArrayReduce[f, array, {{n1, n2}}] (* combine dimensions first *)
ArrayReduce[Mean, m, 1] (* column means *)
ArrayReduce[Max, tensor, 3]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to each 1D (or flattened) slice.

tools.example:
m = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
ArrayReduce[Total, m, 2] (* {6, 15}: row sums *)
ArrayReduce[Total, m, 1] (* {5, 7, 9}: column sums *)
ArrayReduce[Norm, RandomReal[1, {10, 20, 3}], 3] // Dimensions (* {10, 20} *)

tools.name: NestGraph
tools.description: NestGraph[f, expr, n] repeatedly applies f (which returns one or several successors) and builds the graph of all expressions reached within n steps, merging repeated states - state-space exploration, call graphs, Collatz-type maps, rewriting systems; use VertexLabels -> "Name" to label vertices. NestTree (listed) builds a tree instead of merging repeated states.
tools.usage:
NestGraph[f, expr, n]
NestGraph[f, {e1, e2, ...}, n]
NestGraph[f, expr, n, VertexLabels -> "Name"]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function returning a successor or a list of successors.

tools.name: AllMatch
tools.description: AllMatch[list, patt] yields True if every element matches a pattern, AnyMatch if at least one does and NoneMatch if none does - the pattern-based versions of AllTrue/AnyTrue/NoneTrue (listed), with level specifications and operator forms. Use them for structural validation such as checking that all elements are {_String, _Integer} pairs.
tools.usage:
AllMatch[list, patt]
AllMatch[patt][list]
AllMatch[expr, patt, level]
AnyMatch[list, patt]
NoneMatch[list, patt]
tools.example:
AllMatch[{{"a", 1}, {"b", 2}}, {_String, _Integer}] (* True *)
AnyMatch[data, _Missing | _?(# < 0 &)]
Select[records, AllMatch[Values[#], _?NumericQ] &]

tools.name: SelectFirst
tools.description: SelectFirst[list, crit] returns the first element satisfying a predicate (with an optional default when none does) and FirstPosition the position of the first element matching a pattern; both stop scanning at the first hit, unlike Select/Position, and have operator forms. FirstCase (listed) is the pattern-with-replacement variant.
tools.usage:
SelectFirst[list, crit]
SelectFirst[list, crit, default]
SelectFirst[crit][list]
FirstPosition[expr, patt]
FirstPosition[expr, patt, default]
FirstPosition[expr, patt, default, levelspec]

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Value returned when nothing matches (default Missing["NotFound"]).

tools.example:
SelectFirst[{1, 3, 8, 5}, EvenQ] (* 8 *)
SelectFirst[records, #["id"] == 42 &, None]
FirstPosition[{a, b, c, b}, b] (* {2} *)

tools.name: AddTo
tools.description: In-place arithmetic assignment operators: x += y (AddTo), x -= y (SubtractFrom), x *= y (TimesBy), x /= y (DivideBy), x++ / ++x (Increment, PreIncrement), x-- / --x (Decrement, PreDecrement), AppendTo/PrependTo for lists and AssociateTo/KeyDropFrom for associations. They modify the variable and return the new (or, for post-increment, old) value; note that AppendTo on large lists in loops is O(n^2) - prefer Sow/Reap or Table.
tools.usage:
x += y
x -= y
x *= y
x /= y
x++
++x
x--
AppendTo[list, elem]
PrependTo[list, elem]
AssociateTo[assoc, key -> val]
KeyDropFrom[assoc, key]

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Symbol (or indexed variable / part) holding a value.

tools.example:
total = 0; Do[total += i^2, {i, 10}]; total
counts = <||>; Scan[(counts[#] = Lookup[counts, #, 0] + 1) &, words]
n = 5; n++ (* returns 5, n is now 6 *)

tools.name: ApplyTo
tools.description: x //= f (ApplyTo) sets x to f[x], the general in-place update operator (12.2+) that complements +=, *= etc.: x //= Sort, x //= DeleteDuplicates, x //= N. Handy for step-by-step data cleaning where a variable is refined repeatedly.
tools.usage:
x //= f
ApplyTo[x, f]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to the current value.

tools.name: CompoundExpression
tools.description: e1; e2; ... (CompoundExpression) evaluates expressions in sequence and returns the last (or Null with a trailing semicolon, which also suppresses output in notebooks). It is the sequencing construct inside Module/Block bodies, Function bodies and one-line scripts; parenthesize when used as a single argument, e.g. Button["go", (a = 1; b = 2)].
tools.usage:
expr1; expr2; expr3
expr;  (* returns Null, no output *)
(expr1; expr2)  (* as a single argument *)
CompoundExpression[e1, e2, ...]
tools.example:
f[x_] := (Print["called"]; x^2)
result = (a = 3; b = 4; Sqrt[a^2 + b^2]) (* 5 *)

tools.name: Break
tools.description: Break[] exits the innermost Do, For, While or Table-like loop immediately, Continue[] skips to the next iteration, and Return[expr] (listed) exits the enclosing function; Goto[tag]/Label[tag] give unstructured jumps within a CompoundExpression (rarely needed). Throw/Catch remain the tool for non-local exits across function boundaries.
tools.usage:
Do[If[cond, Break[]]; body, {i, n}]
While[True, ...; If[done, Break[]]]
Do[If[skip, Continue[]]; body, {i, n}]
Label[tag]
Goto[tag]

tools.name: SlotSequence
tools.description: ## (SlotSequence) stands for the sequence of all arguments of a pure function and ##n for all arguments from the n-th on, complementing # (Slot) for single arguments; with named arguments (Function[{x, y}, ...]) and #name for association keys they cover all ways of referring to pure-function arguments. Use ## to write variadic wrappers and to forward arguments.
tools.usage:
f[##] &
{##} & [a, b, c]
Plus[##2] & [a, b, c] (* b + c *)
Function[Null, expr, HoldAll] (* held arguments *)
#name & [<|"name" -> 1|>]

tools.name: Distribute
tools.description: Distributes one head over another - Distribute[f[a + b, c + d]] gives f[a, c] + f[a, d] + f[b, c] + f[b, d] - and in particular Distribute[f[{a, b}, {c, d}], List] forms all combinations (a Cartesian product with the head applied), the general form of Tuples/Outer for arbitrary heads; also used to expand tensor/non-commutative products.
tools.usage:
Distribute[expr]
Distribute[expr, g]
Distribute[expr, g, f]
Distribute[f[{a, b}, {c, d}], List]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Head to distribute (default: the outer head).

tools.example:
Distribute[f[a + b, c + d]] (* f[a, c] + f[a, d] + f[b, c] + f[b, d] *)
Distribute[g[{1, 2}, {x, y}], List] (* {g[1, x], g[1, y], g[2, x], g[2, y]} *)

tools.name: Construct
tools.description: Construct[f, x] gives f[x] and Construct[f, x, y] f[x, y] - the explicit function-application function, useful as an argument to Fold, MapThread and Outer when the function is itself data (e.g. Fold[Construct, f, args] builds f[a][b][c] curried applications); Composition and Apply cover the other application patterns.
tools.usage:
Construct[f, x]
Construct[f, x, y, ...]
Fold[Construct, f, {a, b, c}] (* f[a][b][c] *)
MapThread[Construct, {fs, xs}]
tools.example:
MapThread[Construct, {{Sin, Cos, Tan}, {0, 0, 0}}] (* {0, 1, 0} *)
Fold[Construct, Function[x, Function[y, x + y]], {2, 3}] (* 5 *)

tools.name: Unique
tools.description: Generates a new, previously unused symbol (Unique[] gives $nnn, Unique[x] x$nnn, Unique["prefix"] prefixnnn) - the mechanism Module uses for local variables and the tool for generating fresh symbols in code generators and symbolic algorithms; Symbol["name"] and ToExpression create symbols with given names, and Remove deletes them.
tools.usage:
Unique[]
Unique[x]
Unique["prefix"]
Unique[{x, y}]
Unique[x, {Temporary}]

parameters.name: Temporary
parameters.description: Attribute so the symbol is removed when no longer referenced.

tools.example:
vars = Table[Unique["c"], {3}] (* {c1, c2, c3} *)
sol = Solve[Thread[m.vars == b], vars]
Remove /@ vars

tools.name: Function named arguments
tools.description: Beyond # and #1, Function (listed) supports named formal parameters Function[{x, y}, body], attributes as a third argument (Function[{x}, body, HoldAll] for non-evaluating arguments), the \[Function] notation x |-> body (13.0+ typed as |-> ), typed parameters Function[Typed[x, "Real64"], ...] for FunctionCompile, and association slot access #key. This entry summarises those forms, which are essential for readable higher-order code.
tools.usage:
Function[{x, y}, x^2 + y]
x |-> x^2  (* single-argument arrow form *)
{x, y} |-> x + y
Function[{x}, Print[Hold[x]], HoldAll]
Function[Typed[x, "Integer64"], x^2]
#name & /@ records

tools.name: Memoization pattern
tools.description: The idiom f[x_] := f[x] = expr stores each computed value as a DownValue so repeated calls are O(1) (dynamic programming, expensive lookups); combine with Module-scoped caches or Once (listed) for session-level caching, and Clear[f] or ClearAll to reset. Memory grows with the number of distinct arguments, so bound it for unbounded inputs (e.g. cache only small arguments with a Condition).
tools.usage:
f[x_] := f[x] = expr
fib[n_] := fib[n] = fib[n - 1] + fib[n - 2]; fib[0] = 0; fib[1] = 1
g[x_] := g[x] = expensive[x] /; x < 10^4
Clear[f] (* reset cache *)

tools.name: Composition and pipelines
tools.description: Idioms for point-free pipelines: RightComposition (f /* g /* h applies left to right), Composition (f @* g), the postfix operator // for stepwise application, operator forms of most list/string functions (Select[crit], Map[f], SortBy[f], StringCases[patt]), and Through/Comap for fan-out. Prefer /* and operator forms in data-processing code for readability and easy reordering.
tools.usage:
data // Select[Positive] // Map[Sqrt] // Total
pipeline = Select[Positive] /* Map[Sqrt] /* Total
pipeline[data]
(f @* g)[x] (* f[g[x]] *)
Comap[{Min, Max}, data]

tools.name: ReverseApplied
tools.description: ReverseApplied[f] is f with its arguments in reverse order (ReverseApplied[f, n] for exactly n arguments), useful to turn a comparison or binary operation around for Sort, Fold and MapThread without writing a pure function.
tools.usage:
ReverseApplied[f][x, y] (* f[y, x] *)
ReverseApplied[f, n]
tools.example:
Sort[{3, 1, 2}, ReverseApplied[Less]] (* {3, 2, 1} *)
Fold[ReverseApplied[Prepend], {}, {1, 2, 3}]

tools.name: CurryApplied
tools.description: CurryApplied[f, n] gives the curried operator form of an n-argument function so that CurryApplied[f, n][x1][x2]...[xn] equals f[x1, ..., xn]; CurryApplied[f, {i1, i2, ...}] chooses the argument order. It manufactures operator forms for functions that lack built-in ones.
tools.usage:
CurryApplied[f, n]
CurryApplied[f, {i1, i2, ...}]
CurryApplied[n][f]
tools.example:
CurryApplied[Plus, 3][1][2][3] (* 6 *)
subtract5 = CurryApplied[Subtract, {2, 1}][5]; subtract5[12] (* 7 *)

tools.name: FoldPairList
tools.description: Cumulative form of FoldPair: applies a function returning {output, newState} to a state and each element, returning the list of outputs (with an optional final function of the last state); the workhorse for stateful sequence transforms such as running encoders, tokenizers and chunking.
tools.usage:
FoldPairList[f, y0, {x1, x2, ...}]
FoldPairList[f, y0, list, g]

tools.name: SequenceFoldList
tools.description: Cumulative form of SequenceFold: generates the full sequence produced by a recurrence whose next term depends on the previous k terms and the next input element, starting from k seed values - a direct encoding of linear/nonlinear recurrences and recursive filters.
tools.usage: SequenceFoldList[f, {y1, ..., yk}, {x1, x2, ...}]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function of the k previous results and the next element.

tools.example: SequenceFoldList[#1 + #2 &, {1, 1}, Table[Null, 8]] (* Fibonacci numbers *)

tools.name: Increment
tools.description: x++ (Increment) adds 1 to the value of x and returns the old value; ++x (PreIncrement) returns the new value; x-- and --x (Decrement, PreDecrement) subtract 1. Used for counters in procedural loops and in Dynamic interfaces.
tools.usage:
x++
++x
x--
--x
Increment[x]

tools.name: Continue
tools.description: Continue[] skips the rest of the current iteration of the innermost Do, For or While loop and proceeds with the next one; Break[] exits the loop entirely. Both are procedural control-flow shortcuts inside loop bodies.
tools.usage:
Do[If[cond, Continue[]]; body, {i, n}]
While[test, ...; If[skip, Continue[]]; ...]
tools.example: Do[If[Mod[i, 3] != 0, Continue[]]; Print[i], {i, 10}] (* prints 3, 6, 9 *)

tools.name: Goto
tools.description: Goto[tag] transfers control to Label[tag] within the same CompoundExpression (procedure body), an unstructured jump retained for translated legacy code and state machines; structured alternatives (While, Break, Throw/Catch, Return) are preferred in new code.
tools.usage:
Label[tag]
Goto[tag]
tools.example: Module[{i = 0}, Label[again]; i++; If[i < 3, Goto[again]]; i] (* 3 *)
